title: Ending on home
summary: Why ending on the 1 or the 5 sounds finished, how tension notes ask questions, and how to end a loop so it comes round cleanly.

steps.title: Home base
steps.body:
Every key has a home note, the **1**. In A minor, that's A. End a phrase on it and it sounds finished, like a full stop.

The **5** (E in A minor) is the other classic ending. It's in the home chord too, so it sounds settled, just a little more open than 1.

The **2**, **4**, **6** and **7** are tension notes. Each sits one step from a home-chord note and leans toward it. End on one and the phrase hangs, like a question with no answer.

The last note of a loop comes right before bar 1 returns. End on 1 or 5 and each pass sounds complete, so the restart sounds intended.
steps.deeper:
The home chord in A minor is **Am**: A, C and E, which are degrees **1**, **3** and **5**. Over that chord those three notes sound at rest, so they're called **stable**. The 1 is the most final of them.

The other four degrees each sit a step away from a home-chord note: 2 (B) between 1 and 3, 4 (D) between 3 and 5, 6 (F) just above 5, and 7 (G) just below 1. That's why each one seems to lean somewhere.

Ending on the 3 (C) also sounds calm, since it's in the home chord. This lesson's check sticks to 1 and 5.

The check reads the note that **starts** last, so a short note after your ending becomes the new ending.

steps.title: Ending on 1, 5, or 2
steps.caption: Same drums, pad (Am, F, Am) and melody each time. Only the very last note changes: A (1), E (5) or B (2). Listen to the moment the loop comes back round.

examples.label: Ends on 1 (A)
examples.explanation: The last note is the home note, over the home chord. Full stop. The loop comes back round and it sounds like a fresh start.

examples.label: Ends on 5 (E)
examples.explanation: Still settled, since E is in the home chord, but a touch more open than A. It sits well into the restart.

examples.label: Ends on 2 (B)
examples.explanation: B is one step above home, and it hangs. It sounds like the phrase wanted one more note, then the loop cuts back in before it gets there.

steps.title: Tension goes in the middle
steps.body:
Tension notes aren't mistakes. They're how a melody asks a question. What matters is where you put them.

Tension at the end of bar 1 and home at the end of bar 2 is call and response: the loop asks, then answers, every pass.

Flip it, home first and tension last, and the loop ends on a question every time round. That can be a deliberate eerie choice, but make it a choice. By default, end home.

Next: the same notes, with the B and the A swapped.
steps.deeper:
A note that hangs at the end of bar 1 has a whole bar to be answered. The same note at the very end of the loop is answered only by bar 1 starting again, which usually doesn't resolve it, unless bar 1 starts a step away, like the F into E in the AAAB example.

Here the call ends on the 2 (B) and the answer on the 1 (A). Any tension note can end a call: in the last lesson the call ended on the 4 (D).

Unresolved endings are a real style tool: a loop that never settles can feel restless or eerie. The point is to do it on purpose.

steps.title: Where the tension goes
steps.caption: Same drums and pad, same notes in both. The only change: which bar ends on B (2) and which ends on A (1).

examples.label: Tension, then home
examples.explanation: Bar 1 ends on B and hangs. Bar 2 ends on A and answers it. Every pass asks and resolves.

examples.label: Home, then tension
examples.explanation: Bar 1 ends on A, so the question is answered before it's asked. Bar 2 ends on B, so every pass finishes on a question.

steps.title: Land it home
steps.prompt:
Write a melody across **both bars** and make the **last note** a **1** or a **5** (A or E in A minor). The keyboard shows the degree on each key.

Try a call and response: let bar 1 end on a tension note, then land bar 2 home. Press play and listen to the moment the loop comes back round.
hints: Find the keys marked **1** and **5** (A and E in A minor). In the piano roll, put your final note on one of those rows, near the end of bar 2. The home row has the strongest tint.
The check reads the note that **starts** last. If a short note comes after your ending, it becomes the ending: delete it or move it earlier.
Need a shape? Bar 1: degrees 5, 4, 3, then hold the 2. Bar 2: the same rhythm with 4, 3, 2, then hold the 1. In A minor that's E D C B, then D C B A.

steps.message: Practice rep, so nothing goes into Your Track. Next lesson you'll find the melody you keep, and you'll know how to end it.
